item.title: Paytm Lines Up ₹200 Cr Investment in Singapore’s Funding Societies
item.dc:creator: Akshit Pushkarna
item.description: Adding to its international expedition, fintech major Paytm’s board has now approved an investment of up to ₹200 Cr in…
item.content:encoded:
Adding to its international expedition, fintech major Paytm’s board has now approved an investment of up to ₹200 Cr in subsidiaries of Singapore-based Funding Asia Group, also known as Funding Societies.

The proposed investment will be made through its wholly owned subsidiary Paytm Singapore. This includes an initial investment of approximately ₹162 Cr (SGD 21.8 Mn) to acquire a 19.1% stake in CardUp, Funding Societies’ payments subsidiary.

The remaining ₹38 Cr may be invested in one of Funding Societies’ affiliates, Paytm said in a stock exchange filing on Thursday.

With regulatory approvals in place, the company expects to complete the acquisition by May 2027.

Digital payments segment CardUp, incorporated in Singapore in October 2015, allows individuals and businesses to pay large or recurring expenses using a credit card, even where credit cards are normally not accepted. Its turnover has grown consistently over the past three calendar years, rising 53.9% to ₹299.2 Cr in CY25 from ₹194.38 Cr in CY24. The company reported a turnover of ₹104.16 Cr in CY23.

Alongside the proposed investment, Paytm will also enter a five-year business and tech partnership with CardUp, under which it will provide payments and lending technology to the Singapore-based company.

Paytm will earn technology fees and a share of revenue under the arrangement. The partnership is aimed at expanding Paytm’s tech-led payments and financial services stack in Singapore.

The arrangement is part of Paytm’s previously outlined ‘Partner Operated’ strategy for international expansion. Under this model, Paytm and its subsidiaries provide their payments acceptance platform and devices, while local partners handle sales, distribution and on-ground merchant operations.

The model allows Paytm to monetise its technology through licensing fees, revenue-sharing and other arrangements, while limiting the capital required for overseas expansion.

Separately, Paytm announced that it has completed an additional investment of ₹500 Cr in its wholly owned subsidiary, Paytm Cloud Technologies Limited (PCTL). In turn, PCTL invested another ₹500 Cr in Paytm Singapore, taking forward the capital infusion plan disclosed by the company on October 26.

Paytm has been exploring international opportunities alongside improving its overall financial performance in recent times. Its net profit for the September quarter surged 10.7X YoY to ₹225 Cr while its operating revenue for the quarter zoomed 28% YoY and 8% QoQ to ₹2,648 Cr. 

Shares of Paytm ended today’s trading session 8.51% lower at ₹1,727.70 apiece on the BSE.

item.title: Can ShareChat’s Microdrama-Fuelled Revival Keep Going?
item.dc:creator: Meha Agarwal
item.description: A thousand crores in annual revenue is a significant milestone for any Indian consumer internet company. And yet, crossing that…
item.content:encoded:
A thousand crores in annual revenue is a significant milestone for any Indian consumer internet company. And yet, crossing that mark has left ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV parent Mohalla Tech with a few more questions to deal with in the next year or two.

In FY26, the company crossed ₹1,000 Cr in operating revenue for the first time, reporting ₹1,016.27 Cr, a 40.5% increase over the previous year. Yet its net loss widened to ₹1,978.40 Cr, raising an obvious question about the quality of that growth. 

Having said that, a large part of this loss came from share-based payments, which climbed 302% to ₹739 Cr in FY26 from ₹183.8 Cr in FY25, following an expansion of the company’s ESOP pool and additional grants to key employees.

Whether the company crosses the profitability barrier in FY27 will be clear in about a year’s time, but what we know is that with ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV as its three products, ShareChat’s revenue story is changing. 

Mohalla Tech’s legacy chatroom business (ShareChat), built on in-app purchases and microtransactions continues to remain the biggest contributor, bringing in ₹471.76 Cr, but an acceleration was seen in subscription revenue for Moj and QuickTV, which resulted in a ₹292.72 Cr boost to the topline. Advertising revenue, once central to Mohalla Tech’s monetisation ambitions, took a backseat and declined to ₹251.79 Cr.

In other words, the company behind ShareChat and Moj is no longer relying on external revenue levers such as brand partnerships and creators, but is looking to bring in more consistent revenue by selling short-form digital entertainment and microdramas. 

The diversification was not on the cards when it all began in 2015. Ankush Sachdeva, Bhanu Pratap Singh and Farid Ahsan founded ShareChat to tap into the regional language internet boom in India. When TikTok’s ban in 2020 opened the door to short video, ShareChat launched Moj and then later acquired MX TakaTak. Today, it is riding the microdrama wave with QuickTV.   

It is monetising conversations, selling advertising against free content and charging consumers directly for microdramas. But there’s one crucial missing link and that’s to do with how the three main products acquire customers and therein lies a challenge for Mohalla Tech to fix in the long run. 

The company, once valued at around $5 Bn, is reportedly eyeing a $400 Mn IPO in late 2027, subject to achieving a full year of operating profitability in FY27.

The company has seen all from layoffs, leadership exits and cost reductions, forcing the company to shift its focus from audience growth to monetisation and profitability. Now, the question is whether ShareChat’s new revenue mix represents a clearing towards a path to profitability or is it a temporary shift before the next product comes along, as we have seen throughout the company’s lifetime. 

Subscriptions Turn Fruitful 

When QuickTV launched in February 2025, ShareChat was entering a new territory, chasing subscription revenue. Thus far in its lifetime, it relied on incidental revenue in its apps, whether it was in-app transactions by users or ad revenue from brands. QuickTV was the first push for direct revenue. 

And it seems to be working for Mohalla Tech. In FY26, subscriptions accounted for almost the entire increase in the company’s consolidated revenue from operations. 

Cofounder and CFO Manohar Charan revealed in a recent press and investor briefing that subscription had become the company’s clear third revenue stream after a great start.

“And to be honest, that was the single largest force moving our revenue between last year and this year,” Charan said after the FY26 results were announced in early November 2026. 

Besides QuickTV, the company also offers paid subscriptions through Moj Premium, but the latter is not yet a compelling revenue line. Microdrama seems to have hit the ground running. 

However, building a subscription business comes with a different set of challenges, particularly when it comes to acquiring paying customers.

Charan claimed that while Moj spends around ₹14–15 to get a user to download the app, QuickTV subscription platforms can spend 6-7x higher to acquire a paying customer as the cost can be recouped through the subscription model. 

This makes it easier to acquire users profitably over the short term but more expensive over a long period. That long-term cost can take a toll on QuickTV and other microdrama platforms. Subscription-centric apps like microdrama platforms have to continuously invest in content to retain customers, and this can get especially expensive when there are multiple apps competing and offering similar microdramas and storylines. 

While AI is actively changing how microdramas are being made and therefore reducing costs, the economics are still not in the favour of the platform. It is estimated that producing a minute of microdrama using human actors costs ₹20,000–₹25,000, compared with ₹7,000–₹8,000 using AI tools and generative video models. 

While lower production costs could help platforms scale their content libraries and reduce long-term retention costs, they could also make it easier for competitors to produce similar shows, putting greater pressure on differentiation and even that initial customer acquisition. 

QuickTV operates on a commissioned-content model, with the company producing or commissioning around 30–40 shows every month. According to Charan, the QuickTV library has grown to roughly 1,000 shows. 

Moj, meanwhile, relies heavily on creator-generated content, receiving around 4,000 shows daily and offering a catalogue of approximately 5 Lakh shows across formats. The latter also gives Mohalla Tech an opportunity to identify popular themes and formats before committing larger production budgets.

Charan said QuickTV has operated without burning cash since launch, though this remains to be verified since we were not given exact costs for QuickTV in terms of marketing and promotional spends. 

But Mohalla Tech is at a crossroads right now because of how QuickTV has performed. 

Subscriptions have revived its topline growth, but sustaining that momentum will require investing in retargeting, a clear content strategy and pipeline as well as other incremental spending to improve the subscriber experience, which will play a role in retention. 

If the past year has shown anything it is that users will pay for microdramas, but to keep them paying every month requires a lot more pieces moving in sync than just the right marketing pitch.

Microdramas Fuel ShareChat’s Advertising Recovery

Advertising, ShareChat’s other established revenue stream, faced a sharp slowdown in FY26. Revenue declined 13.1% to ₹251.79 Cr in FY26 from ₹289.83 Cr in FY25. The CFO attributed the advertising decline to the loss of real-money gaming advertisers following regulatory changes.

Further, the company says advertising has begun recovering in FY27, supported by higher engagement and stronger monetisation. In Q2 FY27, advertising revenue is said to have grown by 40% YoY, while average ad revenue per user on Moj is claimed to have increased almost 2.5 times since May 2026.

“We are seeing stronger monetisation from our existing user base, and will continue to prioritise investments that drive sustainable engagement and revenue without compromising profitability,” Charan added.

He expects full-year FY27 advertising revenue to exceed ₹350 Cr, but the run rate is not a full-year result and the outlook remains subject to seasonal demand.

Free, ad-supported microdramas are central to boosting ad revenue. It is a clear strategy for Mohalla Tech if it gets its user acquisition right. This will allow the company to keep its ad inventory up-to-date and bring in more consistent revenue outside of the peak seasons. 

When it comes to QuickTV, AI is becoming central to monetisation and bringing in cost-efficiency on the production side. Not only is it playing a role in improving content discovery and therefore driving conversions to subscriptions, but it can help improve ad targeting. 

Charan said an ad-supported model could recover around 2.5 times user acquisition cost over 12 months, compared with roughly 1.6 times for a cautiously run subscription model. Moj was approaching ₹200 in annual advertising revenue per user, against the CFO’s estimate of ₹200–₹250 for YouTube in India. Though this number cannot be verified as YouTube’s average ad revenue per user is not disclosed.  

ShareChat is also experimenting with how brands advertise within microdramas using integrated storytelling or branded content. Other options include ads between episodes, programmatic inventory and interactive shopping formats backed by marketplaces. 

What Will Carry ShareChat Forward?

Like we mentioned above, the caveat to ShareChat’s return to growth is that it has yet to result in lower losses. Charan attributed the forex losses and roughly ₹548 Cr in interest provisions to dollar-denominated financing instruments, describing the latter as non-cash expenses. However, business development costs also surged to ₹334.80 Cr from ₹43.37 Cr, highlighting the spending pressures accompanying growth.

Charan expects FY27 revenue to exceed ₹1,500 Cr, with approximately ₹25 Cr in full-year EBITDA profit. He also claimed the company used just ₹35 Cr of investor cash in FY26 and has been generating cash since September 2025.

However, sustaining this momentum will become increasingly challenging as competition intensifies. Homegrown microdrama platforms such as EloElo, Kuku TV and Story TV are competing for paying subscribers, while global players including ReelShort and DramaBox are targeting the Indian market. 

Larger entertainment platforms, including JioHotstar, ZEE5 and Amazon MX Player, are also expanding into short-form storytelling. This could push up customer acquisition costs and content spending, particularly for QuickTV’s subscription-led business. 

Consolidation can very well be on the cards as competition intensifies and investors increasingly scrutinise contribution margins. 

As we see with the OTT streaming industry, India is home to around 100 Mn – 150 Mn people who regularly pay for content online and even there a kind of subscription fatigue has set in, with users preferring to stick to one platform or only buying subscriptions through telecom bundles. 

It also adds more pressure on ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV to explore ways in which users can seamlessly switch between streaming, creator-generated content and chatrooms. 

Interestingly, the three Mohalla Tech platforms do not currently act as interconnected funnels. This will be a critical piece of operating leverage for the company in the long run. 

Charan explained that QuickTV primarily targets paying subscribers outside the company’s existing ShareChat and Moj audience, acquiring them through platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and YouTube. Connecting this to the silos of ShareChat and Moj will give the company more bargaining power with advertisers as well as creators.  

This is why while ShareChat, Moj and QuickTV’s growth is undeniable, a stronger push by platforms such as YouTube or Meta could challenge that position because of their incumbency and the inherent moats that come with that position. 

But the milestones of FY26, the revenue trajectory and the fact that the company now reaches millions of social media users more frequently through three different apps offer plenty of reasons for optimism, even amid these questions.

item.title: AI Startup Disseqt AI Raises $8 Mn To Scale International Operations
item.dc:creator: Gaurav Bagur
item.description: Disseqt AI, which builds AI agents for AI governance and testing, has raised $8 Mn (about ₹75 Cr) in a…
item.content:encoded:
Disseqt AI, which builds AI agents for AI governance and testing, has raised $8 Mn (about ₹75 Cr) in a funding round led by Gresham House Ventures. Sure Valley Ventures, Delta Partners, and Enterprise Ireland also participated in the round, along with angel investors like cricketer Rahul Dravid and senior executives from OpenAI, Palo Alto Networks, Salesforce, and Meta. 

The startup plans to use the fresh capital to expand its global enterprise customer base and scale operations across the UK and international markets. 

“Every enterprise is handing real work to AI agents, but very few can prove those agents are safe, fair and within policy. This gap often stops ambitious AI projects from going live, and it is what we built Disseqt to close … This funding lets us bring that standard to more enterprises around the world,” said CEO and cofounder Apoorva Kumar. 

Founded in late 2025 by Kumar, Manish Atri, and Cyril Treacy, Disseqt operates an independent governance and testing layer for enterprise AI agents. Essentially, it ensures that AI systems are behaving as intended and meet regulatory requirements. 

The platform enables compliance, security, and IT teams to test agentic workflows for vulnerabilities and data-leak risks prior to deployment. It can enforce real-time policy guardrails in production, block non-compliant outputs, and maintain audit trails independent of underlying model providers. 

While its commercial operations and headquarters are in Ireland, Disseqt’s engineering and AI teams are based in Bengaluru. It has customer-facing operations across the UK, Ireland and India, according to its website. Atri, its COO, is also India-based. Both Kumar and Atri are graduates of IIIT Allahabad. 

Besides, it has also partnered with major Indian IT companies like Infosys, Cognizant, HCLTech, Mphasis, and Tata Technologies as ‘Global System Integrators’ to deploy its platforms for their enterprise clients. 

This adds to the uptick in investor interest in AI startups. As per Inc42’s Indian Tech Startup Funding Report Q3 2026, AI startup funding more than tripled YoY to $438 Mn in the September quarter. The surging investor interest in AI comes even as the overall funding landscape remains relatively subdued, with the cumulative funding raised by Indian startups increasing by just 5% YoY.

item.title: Razorpay To File UDRHP By Next Week, Eyes IPO By February 2027: Report
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Fintech major Razorpay is reportedly looking to file its updated DRHP as early as next week, following the SEBI clearance…
item.content:encoded:
Fintech major Razorpay is reportedly looking to file its updated DRHP as early as next week, following the SEBI clearance for its confidential filing.

The Bengaluru-based startup is eyeing a potential market debut as early as February 2027, Bloomberg reported, adding that it is expected to begin investor roadshows immediately after the public filing.

Inc42 has reached out to Razorpay for comment on the development. The story will be updated upon receiving a response.

The report comes within days after the market regulator cleared the ₹6,000 Cr IPO that could potentially value Razorpay at around $5 Bn (₹47,000 Cr). Pertinent to note that IPO valuation is about 33% lower than the $7.5 Bn valuation it commanded in its last funding round in 2021.

Razorpay had confidentially filed its draft IPO papers in June 2026. SEBI issued its observations on the company’s filing on November 3, allowing it to proceed with the public issue.

Founded in 2014 by Shashank Kumar and Harshil Mathur, Razorpay offers payment processing, business banking, payroll and lending solutions. It raised over $800 Mn from investors including Tiger Global Management, Y Combinator, Ribbit Capital and Lightspeed.

The company reported a 65% YoY increase in operating revenue to ₹3,783 Cr in FY25 but slipped into the red, weighed down by ₹1,209 Cr in ESOP expenses and one-time costs linked to its domicile shift from the US to India. Financial numbers for the period since then would be more apparent when the company files its IPO papers. 

Razorpay is also exploring a 0.4% merchant discount rate (MDR) on eligible UPI transactions above ₹2,000 to boost monetisation. However, its rollout could be delayed until after the 2027 state elections amid concerns over merchant backlash. The central government, RBI and NPCI are yet to finalise an implementation date, despite much of the regulatory groundwork being complete.

Beyond payments, Razorpay is expanding into AI-led products, including its Agent Studio platform for deploying task-specific AI agents.

The company is looking to tap India’s buoyant IPO market, where firms have raised around $18.6 Bn through initial share sales so far in 2026, nearing last year’s record of $22.4 Bn.

item.title: Anthropic IPO Rekindles Debate Over India’s AI Ambitions
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has triggered a debate among Indian business leaders on the country’s ability to build globally competitive AI…
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic’s record-breaking IPO has triggered a debate among Indian business leaders on the country’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies.

Despite rising AI investments in India, the gap in capital, research capabilities and technical talent highlights the challenges facing homegrown AI companies.

Indian AI startups raised $676 Mn across 57 deals in H1 2026, over 4X the year-ago period, but building a global AI giant will require deeper pools of capital, sustained R&D and stronger technical talent.

Anthropic’s stock market debut has offered a glimpse of the extraordinary investor appetite for AI. The Claude parent priced its shares at $83 for the IPO, above its price range of $70-78. The IPO, which values the company at around $1.5 Tn, was oversubscribed by over 10X.

The listing is a landmark moment for the AI industry and gave public market investors an opportunity to back one of the companies at the centre of the AI race.

For scale, Anthropic’s $1.5 Tn IPO valuation is equivalent to nearly 37% of India’s projected nominal GDP of $4.06 Tn for FY27, as per the IMF’s October estimates.

However, the significance of this IPO extends beyond Wall Street. In India, it has sparked a debate about the country’s ability to build globally competitive AI companies.

The conversation gained momentum after veteran banker and Kotak Mahindra Bank founder Uday Kotak compared Anthropic’s valuation with the combined market capitalisation of India’s top 10 companies. In a post on X, he questioned whether Indian businesses were undervalued or whether the country needed to catch up with the new tech economy.

“Anthropic, an AI company known for Claude, listed at a valuation of $1.5 Tn. It did not exist until about 5 years ago. This is more than the combined market cap of the top 10 Indian companies. Are we undervalued, or do we need to catch up in the new world? Or both?” Kotak wrote.

The debate that unfolded after this comparison saw Adani Group CFO Jugeshinder Robbie Singh label the Anthropic IPO as a “textbook category error in asset pricing”. In a post on X titled “Cross-Regime Category Error: Why Legacy Bankers Can’t Price Synthetic GDP”, Singh argued that India’s largest companies and frontier AI businesses operate in fundamentally different economic regimes.

“India’s blue chips are neither undervalued nor ‘behind’ — they are yield vehicles monetising the physical human economy,” he wrote, arguing that frontier AI companies are being valued for their potential to create “synthetic GDP” through autonomous AI agents and digital workforces.

Ex-Infosys CFO Mohandas Pai questioned the premise of comparing the two. “Every disruption creates new companies with huge valuations. It is the nature of markets. Comparing is silly,” he wrote.

Pai argued that the more pertinent question the IPO raises for India is what exactly is needed for an Indian company to recreate an Anthropic-like scale.

This reflects a broader question prevalent in the Indian startup ecosystem: whether the country can move beyond valuing existing businesses to fostering innovation and funding deeptech companies that may take years to build.

The question gains more significance as funding for Indian AI startups gathers pace despite lagging significantly behind global levels.

More Money Flows, But The Gap Remains

AI emerged as the defining theme in the Indian startup ecosystem in Q3 2026, with startups in the segment raising a record $438 Mn, up 265% YoY, across 35 deals. This took the sector’s total funding in the first nine months of 2026 to more than $1.1 Bn.

The surge stands out against a relatively subdued funding environment. Indian startups collectively raised $2.2 Bn across 210 deals in Q3, up just 5% YoY, while the deal count fell 13%.

However, the increase in AI funding has also brought valuations under scrutiny. Inc42’s Indian Investor Ranking & Sentiment Survey, based on responses from more than 85 institutional investors, found that 63% of investors see some degree of froth in Indian AI startup valuations. About half expect a correction within the next 18 months.

Pranav Obhrai, founding and managing partner at Atrium Ventures, said rising AI valuations are part of a global trend, particularly in the US. He added that vertical AI applications offer a clearer path to building defensible businesses through distribution.

“Distribution becomes the moat, especially in India, where technology alone offers limited protection against global competition,” he said.

Vertical AI applications across BFSI, healthcare, defence and agriculture emerged as the top choice in Inc42’s survey, with 39% of investors expecting them to capture the most value over the next five years. AI hardware and semiconductors followed at 23%, while AI-led IT and business services accounted for 18%.

The findings suggested that investors were increasingly prioritising commercially viable AI applications over capital-intensive foundational technology. Whether the funding momentum continues will depend on sustainable revenue, defensible businesses and valuations that can withstand a potential correction.

What Will It Take To Build India’s Next AI Giant?

Capital alone, however, will not be enough. Building deeptech companies capable of locking horns with giants like Anthropic also requires research talent, technical expertise and the infrastructure to train and run increasingly sophisticated models.

An analysis by General Catalyst’s Utkarsh Bajpai of companies valued at over $5 Bn highlighted the role of technical talent in value creation. Researchers lead 16% of these companies but account for 31% of their combined $170 Bn valuation. Nearly 80% of the founders have technical backgrounds.

For Indian startups, this means moving beyond products that merely package existing foundation models. As access to these models becomes easier, differentiation will increasingly hinge on proprietary technology, domain expertise and solutions to specific problems.

“Gone are the days when you could just build wrappers on top of foundational models. You have to build vertically focused products that solve real problems with an AI-first approach,” Mehta said.

The opportunity extends beyond large language models to AI applications, enterprise software, robotics and other deeptech segments. But building globally competitive businesses in these areas requires patient capital and sustained investment in research, talent and infrastructure, often years before commercial returns materialise.

India’s challenge, therefore, is to move from participating in the AI market to building technology that competes globally. Rising funding signals investor interest, but translating it into durable businesses will require stronger research capabilities, technical talent and a willingness to back ambitious ideas for the long term.

Edited by Akshit Pushkarna

item.title: NEPRA Raises ₹110 Cr To Expand Plastic Recycling Capacity
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: Ahmedabad-based waste management startup NEPRA has raised ₹110 Cr (about $11.7 Mn) in an equity funding round from the Private…
item.content:encoded:
Ahmedabad-based waste management startup NEPRA has raised ₹110 Cr (about $11.7 Mn) in an equity funding round from the Private Infrastructure Development Group (PIDG), a London-based infrastructure development and finance organisation, through its project development arm InfraCo.

The company, which operates under the ‘NEPRA – Let’s Recycle’ brand, will use the capital to develop new material recovery facilities (MRFs), expand plastic recycling capacity, strengthen existing operations, and meet working capital requirements.

NEPRA plans to more than double its waste processing capacity from around 900 tonnes per day to 1,880 tonnes. It also aims to increase its plastic recycling capacity from 6,200 tonnes annually to 18,000 tonnes.

According to the announcement, the transaction marks PIDG’s first equity investment in Asia’s waste management and recycling sector. PIDG joins NEPRA’s existing investors, including Aavishkaar Capital, Circulate Capital, Blue Earth Capital, and Asha Impact.

Founded in 2006, NEPRA collects, segregates, processes, and recycles waste. The company says it currently processes more than 900 tonnes of waste daily through its facilities in Ahmedabad, Indore, Pune, and Bengaluru.

It also operates a plastic recycling plant in Sanand, Gujarat, where it converts plastic waste into recycled granules. Non-recyclable waste is processed into refuse-derived fuel (RDF) for use in cement manufacturing.

NEPRA works with brand owners to help them meet extended producer responsibility (EPR) obligations through traceable recycling processes. Its collection network includes more than 1,500 registered waste pickers.

The company previously raised $18 Mn in a Series C round from Aavishkaar Capital and Circulate Capital in November 2020.

Recycling Startups Attract Capital

NEPRA’s fundraise follows investments in other Indian startups building waste collection, processing, and recycling infrastructure.

Earlier this week, Bengaluru-based Recove Ventures raised ₹56.3 Cr through a mix of equity and debt to expand its plastic waste collection, processing, and recycling infrastructure. It plans to invest more than ₹2,000 Cr across Maharashtra, Karnataka, Gujarat, and Uttar Pradesh over the next decade.

Hyderabad-based Recykal also raised $23 Mn in a bridge round, with former cricketer Sachin Tendulkar subsequently joining its cap table. Recykal operates a B2B marketplace for recyclable materials and offers software to help brands track plastic and e-waste recycling.

Beyond plastics, Delhi NCR-based Karo Sambhav raised ₹56 Cr from Rainmatter in June 2026 to expand infrastructure for recovering critical, precious, and high-value materials from end-of-life products.

item.title: InPrime Finserv Raises ₹101 Cr To Expand Lending, Enter Micro-Mortgages
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Bengaluru-based NBFC InPrime Finserv has raised ₹101 Cr (about $10.7 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by Dutch…
item.content:encoded:
Bengaluru-based NBFC InPrime Finserv has raised ₹101 Cr (about $10.7 Mn) in a Series B funding round led by Dutch entrepreneurial development bank FMO, with participation from existing investors Z47 (formerly Matrix Partners India) and Pravega Ventures.

The lender will use the capital to expand its geographical presence, enter the micro-mortgage segment, and strengthen its AI capabilities across underwriting and customer service.

It also plans to increase investments in agentic AI and AI copilots. According to the NBFC, four in-house AI copilots currently support its credit team, while three AI-powered voice agents handled more than 1.26 Lakh customer calls between April and September 2026.

Founded in 2021 by Sneh Thakur, Manish Raj, and Rajat Singh, InPrime began operations in 2023. It lends to small business owners and self-employed individuals, including kirana store owners, dairy farmers, and beauty parlour operators — a customer group it calls the ‘informal prime’ segment.

According to InPrime, these borrowers often run established businesses and own property but struggle to access formal credit, leaving them dependent on multiple lenders to meet their financing needs.

“This funding will help us take that model further, expand our reach and use technology and AI to serve our customers better at scale,” cofounder Singh said.

InPrime combines data-led underwriting with a field team to assess borrowers beyond conventional financial metrics. It said its AI systems help interpret unstructured data and support customer interactions in vernacular languages.

It operates 46 area offices across Karnataka, Uttar Pradesh, Rajasthan, Haryana, Uttarakhand, and Madhya Pradesh. It has served more than 27,000 households and disbursed ₹516.92 Cr in loans to date.

As of September 30, 2026, its assets under management (AUM) stood at ₹332.8 Cr, while its gross non-performing asset (GNPA) ratio was 0.8%.

The latest round takes InPrime’s total funding to ₹190 Cr. Its other investors include Info Edge Ventures, Kettleborough VC, and Titan Capital.

The fundraise follows investments in other fintech companies with lending businesses. Olyv recently raised an additional $6 Mn from Nippon Life India AIF Management and existing investors in an extension of its Series B round. 

In August, global investment firm Prosus invested $100 Mn in Sachin Bansal-led fintech startup Navi, marking the latter’s first institutional fundraise. The investment, which gives Prosus a minority stake in Navi, was cleared by the Competition Commission of India (CCI) last month.

item.title: Nitin Gadkari Urges States To Adopt Aggregator Guidelines Amid Bike Taxi Crackdowns
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Union minister for road transport and highways Nitin Gadkari has urged states to adopt the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025,…
item.content:encoded:
Union minister for road transport and highways Nitin Gadkari has urged states to adopt the Motor Vehicle Aggregator Guidelines, 2025, citing their potential to expand livelihood opportunities amid crackdowns on bike taxi operations across several states.

The remarks came during the ‘RIDE – Moving India Forward’ event in New Delhi, organised in collaboration with Uber, Ola, Rapido, Bharat Taxi, Zomato, Swiggy and Porter.

Gadkari said aggregator platforms have already generated 4 Cr jobs following the introduction of the government’s policy framework, despite its adoption by only two states.

“If the whole country accepts this, then 10 Cr jobs will be created. And the food and other delivery apps working in this are different. So, if 10 Cr and 8-10 Cr are there, then 18 Cr jobs will be created here,” the minister said.

He added that these platforms could generate employment without requiring government capital expenditure. “Not everyone can get a government job. Not even so many governments have jobs,” Gadkari said.

The minister said he has written to state governments, urging them to adopt the framework and enable app-based mobility services to create livelihoods, particularly for people from socially, economically and educationally disadvantaged backgrounds.

He also highlighted the expansion of app-based services beyond passenger transport into food and goods delivery, creating opportunities for employment and entrepreneurship. He cited e-rickshaws and e-carts as examples of technology transforming traditional occupations and reducing physical hardship.

Gadkari further emphasised the need to strengthen last-mile connectivity in rural areas, arguing that better access to transport services could help people travel to schools and cities, while enabling farmers to take their produce to urban markets.

“Children will be able to go to school. They will start coming to the city. If they can bring their milk, fruits, flowers, vegetables to the city, then the economy can change,” he said.

On regulation, he said the ministry’s objective is to support the sector’s growth while protecting drivers and passengers, and called on companies to share suggestions to improve the framework.

“The aim of the ministry is not to control anyone. All of us should come together, think together and work together,” he said.

State-Level Bike Taxi Crackdowns

Gadkari’s push for wider adoption of the aggregator framework comes amid regulatory uncertainty and enforcement action against bike taxi operators across several states.

In Kolhapur, the RTO seized 10 two-wheelers allegedly operating as Rapido bike taxis and said no bike-taxi app had been granted permission to operate in the district.

In Odisha, the Crime Branch directed Uber and Rapido to discontinue their bike taxi services, terming them unauthorised over the alleged commercial use of private, non-transport two-wheelers.

Meanwhile, Karnataka’s bike taxi dispute remains before the Supreme Court, with the state challenging a January 2026 High Court ruling that allowed operations to resume. In August, the state’s transport department inspected 220 two-wheelers in Bengaluru, booked 71 and seized 70.

In May, Maharashtra’s transport minister Pratap Sarnaik urged the state’s cybercrime department to shut down bike taxi services operated by Ola, Uber and Rapido and file FIRs against their management.

What The Guidelines Cover

Issued on July 1, 2025, under Section 93 of the Motor Vehicles Act, 1988, the guidelines provide a framework for states to license and regulate aggregators.

They prescribe five-year licences, a ₹5 Lakh grant fee and security deposits of ₹10-50 Lakh, depending on fleet size. Surge pricing is capped at twice the base fare, while drivers using their own vehicles must receive at least 80% of the applicable fare.

Aggregators must provide ₹5 Lakh health insurance and at least ₹10 Lakh term insurance for drivers. Requirements also cover training, tracking, panic buttons, round-the-clock support and grievance redressal. Drivers can work across platforms.

Clause 23 lets states permit private motorcycles to carry passengers through aggregators under Section 67(3), subject to driver checks, licensing, insurance and training. States may levy daily, weekly or fortnightly fees.

This is optional, rather than nationwide permission for private bike taxis. Other aggregator vehicles require applicable permits, including contract carriage permits for cars carrying paying passengers. 

Subsequent amendments allow apps to offer voluntary tipping only after a trip, with the entire amount credited to the driver. They also require an option to choose a driver of the same gender, wherever available, including female drivers for women passengers.

item.title: August AI Raises $12 Mn To Expand AI Healthcare Assistant In The US
item.dc:creator: Anjali Jain
item.description: AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its…
item.content:encoded:
AI healthtech startup August AI has raised $12 Mn from Accel, Peak XV Partners, and Claypond Capital to expand its healthcare assistant’s ability to book appointments, find medicines, and follow up on insurance claims for users in the US.

Founder and CEO Anuruddh Mishra announced the fundraise on social media alongside the rollout of the new capabilities. The startup claims to have helped 10 Mn people understand their health through its AI companion.

The development comes after Inc42 exclusively reported in August that the startup was in talks to raise around $4 Mn from Peak XV Partners, with the terms still under discussion.

August AI previously raised $3 Mn in seed funding from Accel and Claypond Capital, the family office of Manipal Group chairman Ranjan Pai, in October 2025.

Founded in 2022 by IIT-BHU alumnus Mishra, August AI initially built an AI-powered health companion to help users understand symptoms, prescriptions, medications, and medical reports. The platform also offers personalised health insights, nutrition guidance, and medication reminders.

It is now extending its offering to tasks patients must complete to access care, from finding a doctor covered by their insurance to locating prescribed medicines.

According to Mishra, the AI agent calls doctors’ offices, checks availability, and books the earliest available appointment with the user’s approval. It can also call nearby pharmacies to compare medicine availability and prices, review medical bills for potential errors and savings, and follow up with insurers and hospitals on denied claims.

The new capabilities are available in beta in the US, with users able to join a waitlist for access.

Mishra said August AI spent 24,286 minutes on hold while finding in-network doctor appointments for early users over the past few weeks. This included 366 minutes for a single user. He also claimed the platform helped another user save $1,255 on an insurance claim.

The administrative assistant builds on the startup’s existing US healthcare offering. In September, August AI launched August Care, a $39-a-month membership offering telehealth consultations, discounted laboratory tests, prescription services, and insurance guidance. The company says licensed physicians make clinical decisions within the service. 

August AI’s expansion comes amid increased investor interest in startups using AI to manage healthcare workflows, both for patients and providers.

In September, Bengaluru-based Prodoc AI raised a seed round to develop agentic AI solutions for hospital workflows, including patient engagement, appointment conversion and care coordination. 

Meanwhile, US-based Confido Health raised $12.5 Mn in an extension round led by Z47 in October to expand its AI agents for appointment scheduling, insurance verification, prescription refills and other administrative tasks.

item.title: UPI MDR Rollout May Be Pushed Beyond 2027 State Polls: Report
item.dc:creator: Palak Sharma
item.description: The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be delayed until after the 2027 state…
item.content:encoded:
The introduction of a merchant discount rate (MDR) on select UPI transactions could be delayed until after the 2027 state elections, with the government concerned about a potential backlash from merchants and trade associations.

Citing industry sources, Financial Express reported that the government, RBI, and National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) are yet to agree on an implementation date, despite much of the regulatory and operational groundwork being complete.

Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, Uttarakhand, Goa, and Manipur are due to go to polls in the first half of next year. A senior industry official cited by the publication described a deferment until after the Uttar Pradesh polls as a worst-case scenario.

Discussions remain focused on finding a suitable rollout window. While minor modifications are possible after implementation, the official ruled out substantial changes to the framework.

MDR is a fee charged to merchants for processing payments. Under the proposed framework, eligible person-to-merchant (P2M) UPI transactions above ₹2,000 would attract a 0.4% charge, capped at ₹300 for transactions of ₹75,000 and above. Transactions of up to ₹2,000, person-to-person transfers, and eligible small-merchant transactions would remain exempt.

The rollout was initially scheduled for October 15 but was deferred until after Diwali, with NPCI citing the festive season. The payments body said it would notify a revised implementation date separately.

Meanwhile, NPCI has notified the UPI Vyapaar Saksham scheme, which will use a portion of MDR collections to support QR code and soundbox deployment among small merchants. The scheme will run for three years from the implementation of UPI MDR.

Shares of fintech companies Paytm, Pine Labs, and MobiKwik fell sharply in morning trade following the report of a possible further delay in MDR rollout. At 11:05 AM IST, the stocks were trading around 9%, 5%, and 7% lower, respectively.

During the session, Paytm parent One 97 Communications fell as much as 9.1% to ₹1,715, while Pine Labs declined 5.5% to ₹159.90. MobiKwik parent One MobiKwik Systems dropped as much as 8.7% to ₹206.80.

item.content:encoded:
Humyn Labs’s $47 Mn Physical AI Play

Humyn Labs is capitalising on the physical AI gold rush. The startup has raised $47 Mn, via debt and equity, to scale its business of recording humans for training robots. As questions over privacy and consent linger, how is Humyn Labs building its warchest to dominate physical AI?

Funding Global Ambition: The round comprised $26 Mn in equity investment, which was led by Accel. The remaining $21 Mn was raised via debt from Lighthouse Canton and Trifecta Capital. The infusion will go towards expanding robot deployment operations to Brazil, South Korea and India, while strengthening its data collection hardware and processing capabilities. The corpus will also help scale the startup’s presence in San Francisco, London and Seoul.

A Rapid Rise: Founded earlier this year, the startup claims to have already $50 Mn in ARR within six months of operation. This pace of growth, coupled with the burgeoning physical AI data collection market, appears to have caught the attention of global investors. But the bigger ace up the startup’s sleeve is its tech stack and the scale of its operations. 

A Sprawling Empire: Humyn Labs has developed its own two-camera hardware to record people performing everyday tasks. It then uses its software to process and label the footage, which is then used by robots for training. Overall, its data collection operations span more than 20 countries across Latin America and Asia.

The Contradictory Core: Beyond the headlines, the startup’s business model has raised serious questions around privacy, consent and data ownership. Recordings inside homes and factories could capture personal information, which has made consent and storage safeguards critical. Even deeper lies a stark labour paradox: workers are recording the very movements that will be used to train machines designed to automate their jobs.

Amid this backdrop, it will be interesting to see how Humyn Labs balances privacy safeguards, data usage and fair compensation. While that is a story for another day, here is all about Humyn Labs’ $47 Mn round…

From The Editor’s Desk

From Blinkit To Vice City

  • The quick commerce platform has started delivering download codes for Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA 6) in select areas across 11 Indian cities. The company plans to expand availability to more cities between November 18 and 19.
  • The deliveries will see customers receive a physical box containing a digital download code for the game, rather than a traditional game disc. Buyers can redeem the code through the PlayStation Store and unlock the game.
  • This comes as the Indian quick commerce market is projected to reach $40 Bn by 2030, driven by hyperlocal fulfillment, convenience and rising disposable incomes. 

Inside The Optimizely Hack

  • The digital experience platform has been hit by a major data breach. Cyberattackers compromised customer projects on Optimizely Web and then used the platform’s content delivery network to distribute malware. 
  • This hack affected 178 companies including the likes of Zoom, BBC, CNN, Salesforce, GitLab and IKEA. The company has acknowledged the hack and claims to have already deployed a fix to fully remediate the vulnerability.
  • The malware could also scan webpages for wallet addresses and substitute them with attacker-controlled ones, supporting Bitcoin and Ethereum. The attackers are said to have stolen nearly $7,151 via this method. 

Xiaomi’s Royalty Bill Comes Due

  • Indian tax authorities are seeking to recover unpaid customs duties and penalties from the Chinese smartphone maker. The matter in question could potentially cost the OEM’s India business more than $150 Mn.
  • Officials argue that Xiaomi’s royalty payments to vendors should be included in the value of imported components while calculating customs duties. The OEM claims that the parts were imported by its vendors and that royalties should not attract custom duties.
  • This comes a couple of months after the SFIO recommended a detailed probe into alleged irregularities in Xiaomi’s business operations and possible FEMA violations. The OEM was earlier also probed for illegally remitted funds overseas in the name of royalty.

Enerzolve Eyes $20 Mn

  • The deeptech startup is in talks to raise around $16- 20 Mn (₹150-186 Cr) in a fresh round, which will likely be led by existing backer Jungle Ventures. There is also a possibility of a new investor joining the startup’s cap table.
  • Founded in 2024, Enerzolve builds hardware and embedded systems for smart grids, renewable energy infrastructure and battery storage. It also offers original design manufacturing and customised engineering solutions for industrial players.
  • The planned fundraise comes as the expansion of renewable energy capacity, smart meter deployments and battery energy storage projects is creating demand for local power electronics and grid management solutions.

Airtel Payments Bank’s Q2 Show

  • The payments bank’s net profit zoomed 139% YoY to ₹28.2 Cr in Q2 FY27 on the back of revenues rising nearly 9% YoY to ₹875.5 Cr, improving margins and growing adoption of its services. Meanwhile, EBITDA zoomed 39.4% YoY to ₹124.5 Cr.
  • On the operational front, the payments bank said that its monthly transacting users (for savings bank account) grew 21.1% YoY to 3.1 Cr during the quarter under review, while customer balances grew 10% YoY to nearly ₹4,385 Cr.
  • Airtel Payments Bank commenced operations in early 2017 with a seed investment of $440 Mn. It was the only profitable payments bank in the country in Q2 FY27 as rival Fino Payments Bank slipped into the red during the quarter. 

Inc42 Markets

Inc42 Startup Spotlight

How Patang Is Putting Regional Indian Snacks On The Shelves

India’s culinary diversity is vast, but its snack aisle rarely reflects it. Popular regional treats are either unavailable outside their home markets or are reformulated for mass production. Enter Patang, a D2C brand that wants to make authentic regional snacks accessible across the country.

Delicacies At Doorsteps: Founded in 2025, Patang sells regional snacks such as Ratlami Sev, Jamnagari Chiwda, Jaipur Hing Chana, Darbhanga Makhana and Kollam Puli Inji. It partners with more than 20 manufacturing kitchens across India to bring these regional savouries to a wider market. 

Made At Source: Instead of using a central industrial kitchen, Patang follows a decentralised model. It sources ingredients regionally and prepares products in small batches close to their places of origin. Final packaging and quality control are undertaken near Delhi. It oversees spice specifications, ingredients  and batch checks to maintain consistency. 

Patang’s Flavour Map: With 22 SKUs under its belt, the startup claims to have so far served more than 15,000 customers. It reported gross margins of around 70% in FY26 and monthly revenue growth of 43%. The brand now plans to expand into spices and condiments, strengthen sales and eventually enter markets with large Indian diaspora populations. 

With India’s snack market projected to become a $43 Bn opportunity by 2032, can Patang turn local snacks into a national craving?

item.title: Mufin Green Finance To Buy 23% Stake In BimaPay For ₹66 Cr
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42

item.content:encoded:
Listed non-banking financial company (NBFC) Mufin Green Finance’s board has approved the acquisition of a 23% stake in insurtech startup BimaPay for a ₹65.8 Cr in an all-cash deal. 

Mufin Green Finance said that it expects to complete the transaction in the next three to four months, subject to the execution of definitive agreements and relevant regulatory approvals. It is pertinent to note that BimaPay operates under the umbrella of the broader Mufin Group. 

“…. With an RBI-registered NBFC as a shareholder, we can build products around how lending actually works rather than adapt them later,” said BimaPay cofounder and CEO Hanut Mehta. 

In a statement, Mufin said that he proposed investment will leverage synergies between the two entities and support the joint development and scaling of premium financing solutions. The transaction will look to combine the listed NBFC’s lending expertise with BimaPay’s tech solutions. 

“… An ownership stake lets us plan product, data and integration roadmaps over years instead of project cycles, which is what a lender growing at our pace needs,” added Mufin Green Finance managing director Kapil Garg said.

The deal is a related-party transaction as Bimapay is a promoter-group subsidiary of Mufin, the listed NBFC said.

Founded in 2022 by Mehta, Mohit Gupta and Kapil Garg, BimaPay facilitates financing solutions to enable individuals and businesses to pay insurance premiums in EMIs instead of upfront lump sums. It also works with lending partners and insurers to develop technology-enabled solutions.

The startup last raised $2 Mn in an undisclosed funding round led by LC Nueva Investment Partners in 2024.

On the financial front BimaPay reported revenue of ₹9.9 Cr in the fiscal year 2025-26 (FY26), up 203% from ₹3.2 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. According to Mufin Green Finance, the startup also reported a profit before tax (PBT) of ₹1.1 Cr in FY26. 

BimaPay operates at the intersection of lending tech and insurtech. The two segments are seeing healthy growth on the back of rising smartphone adoption, expanding credit and the rise of AI-driven distribution solutions.

According to Inc42 data, the Indian insurtech market is projected to become a $307 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.content:encoded:
Moving beyond test preparation, listed edtech major PhysicsWallah (PW) has now said that it is establishing a “greenfield digital” university. 

In an investor presentation, the edtech platform said that the digital university has already been notified by the Punjab government. The digital university plans to offer 16 undergraduate, postgraduate, diploma and certificate courses including BCA, BBA, B.Com, BA, M.Com, MCA, MBA, among others. 

The edtech major also claimed that the nearly 15,000 sq ft campus will be self-financed and will operate on an asset-light model. Admissions are slated to begin in July 2027. The listed company has opted for a digital delivery model that pairs online degrees with competitive exam preparation (such as B.Com-CA and BA-UPSC combinations).

“After Class 12, many learners take a degree elsewhere. PWDU (PW digital university) keeps them with PW, from exam prep to a degree to a career,” read the presentation. 

PW has received authorisation from the state government under the “Punjab Private Digital Open Universities Policy”. The digital university will have a 3 acre physical campus, but it will serve only as the headquarters for administrative purposes. No regular classes will be held on campus.

The announcement came on the same day as the company’s maiden Investor Day in Mumbai. At the event, the company outlined an ambitious target of ₹9,000 Cr to ₹10,000 Cr in revenue by fiscal year 2029-30 (FY30). This implies a 2.5X jump from the ₹3,900 Cr top line that the company reported in FY26

The company expects this growth surge to come on the back of its online business, which it projects will contribute around “two-thirds” of its total revenue by FY30.

At its maiden Investor Day in Mumbai, the edtech giant said that it expects its revenue to rise ‌at ⁠an compounded annual growth rate (CAGR) of more than 25% between FY27 and FY30. It is also targeting an EBITDA ​margin of over 20% by ​FY30.

“Our FY30 ambition is about profit growing faster than revenue. We will stay disciplined with capital and report our progress every year,” said PhysicsWallah chief financial officer (CFO) Amit Sachdeva.

Over the next three to five years, PW plans to focus on premiumisation to drive higher average revenue per user (ARPU), leverage AI to drive efficiencies, scale vernacular courses and tap into the pre-foundation (Class 6 to Class 8) and upskilling markets.

The bullish outlook comes as PW reported a consolidated net profit of ₹143.6 Cr in the second quarter (Q2) of the fiscal year 2026-27 (FY27), up 106% from ₹69.7 Cr in the year-ago quarter. Meanwhile, revenue from operations also rose 18.2% to ₹1,242.3 Cr in the quarter under review from ₹1,051.3 Cr in Q2 FY26.

item.content:encoded:
Omnichannel fast fashion brand Style Union’s parent Nexon Omniverse Ltd has raised ₹485 Cr (nearly $51.8 Mn) in its Series E funding round co-led by Venturi Partners and Elev8 Venture Partners.

In a statement, the platform said that the round comprised both primary and secondary components. Style Union plans to utilise the fresh capital to expand its offline store network across key metros in West and North India.

“This is a defining moment for Nexon Omniverse and for Style Union… With their backing, we will take Style Union beyond its southern base into West and North India and into millions of new households across the country.” said Nexon Omniverse whole-time director Rajesh Seth.

Founded in 2022 by former operations head of Future Retail Rakesh Biyani and his wife Ekta Biyani, Style Union sells apparels for men, women and kids through its own website as well as offline stores. With its core footprint in South India, the brand operates 200 physical stores across Karnataka, Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Kerala, Tamil Nadu, among other cities. 

The platform claims to have closed FY26 with over ₹1,150 Cr in revenue. It competes with the likes of Tata-owned Zudio, V-Mart and Vishal Mega Mart.

The funding comes as a growing number of Indian D2C fashion and lifestyle brands are expanding beyond online channels and building omnichannel businesses. Startups are increasingly using physical stores to improve brand discovery and customer experience while continuing to leverage ecommerce for scale.

On the back of this, the space continues to attract healthy investor interest. In September this year, D2C fashion and accessories brand Theater bagged ₹75 Cr in its Series A round led by investment firm Niveshaay. Earlier this year in March, omnichannel streetwear brand Bonkers Corner also raised $15 Mn to fuel its offline expansion plans.

Prior to this in January, D2C lifestyle brand Salty also raised ₹30 Cr to expand its product portfolio and set up a flagship store.

At the heart of all this is the homegrown fashion ecommerce space, which is projected to become a $112 Bn opportunity by 2030.

item.title: Boba Bhai Bags $18 Mn To Build A Multi-Brand QSR Chain
item.dc:creator: Shrishti Bisht
item.description: Quick service restaurant (QSR) chain Boba Bhai has raised $18 Mn (about ₹168 Cr) in its Series B funding round…
item.content:encoded:
Quick service restaurant (QSR) chain Boba Bhai has raised $18 Mn (about ₹168 Cr) in its Series B funding round led by US-based Left Lane Capital. The round also saw participation from BIG Capital as well as existing backers including Titan Capital. 

Speaking with Inc42, founder Dhruv Kohli said that the round comprised both a primary deal and a small secondary component.

The fresh capital will primarily be deployed towards store expansion, strengthening its senior leadership team and building new consumer food brands under Boba Bhai Ventures.

“Expansion is the sole priority. As we have more capital now, we will double down on existing markets while also entering new markets,” Kohli said.

The latest fundraise comes months after Boba Bhai raised ₹40 Cr in its Series A round in March this year, which was co-led by 8i Ventures, Titan Capital Winners Fund and Global Growth Capital.

Founded in 2023 by Kohli, Boba Bhai is a QSR brand built around Korean delicacies like bubble tea, fusion burgers, ice cream, and fries. It claims to have expanded to 120 locations across India and serves around 3.5 Lakh orders every month. The brand also operates in tier II markets such as Lucknow, Jaipur and Kanpur.

With the latest capital infusion, Boba Bhai aims to more than double its store network to 250-300 outlets over the next 12 months. Kohli identified Kolkata, Ahmedabad and Chandigarh as key markets that Boba Bhai plans to enter over the next three to six months. It will also look at expanding into more tier II and tier III markets, including Nashik.

Boba Bhai currently has its largest store presence in Bengaluru, while Mumbai and Karnal are among its strongest markets in terms of consumer traction, Kohli said.

The startup is also expanding its product portfolio. On the QSR side, the brand claims to have introduced new ramen variants, including Shoyu, peanut and chilli flavours, alongside different protein options such as chicken, vegetarian and mushroom. Ramen currently contributes around 5-5.5% of Boba Bhai’s overall sales. 

On the FMCG side, Boba Bhai has expanded beyond beverages with a snacks range, including Korean chips. The products are being distributed through quick commerce platforms, with the startup recently launching its chips on Blinkit across five cities. 

Boba Bhai is currently clocking nearly 1,500 orders per day via quick commerce channel, said Kohli, adding that the startup now plans to expand its quick commerce presence further.

Building A Multi-Brand F&B Chain

Beyond its flagship Korean-inspired F&B brand, Boba Bhai is also looking to build a broader QSR platform through Boba Bhai Ventures.

The startup has already launched its second brand, Aureco Mexican Kitchen, with two outlets in Bengaluru. The brand is currently in the trial and testing phase, with plans to expand based on consumer response.

Unlike Boba Bhai, which focuses on Korean street food and bubble tea, Aureco will operate as a separate Mexican food brand with its own outlets, team and identity, while remaining under the same parent entity.

Kohli said the startup identified Mexican food as an opportunity to cater to different consumption occasions. While Boba Bhai’s Korean offerings see demand during snack time, evenings, dinner and late-night occasions, the startup saw an opportunity to build a brand catering to lunch consumption.

The founder added that Boba Bhai Ventures could eventually house one or two more large QSR brands, with the potential to scale each to 500-600 outlets.

The startup, however, does not plan to enter categories such as biryani, pizza or traditional Indian food. Instead, it intends to focus on global cuisines and brands targeted at younger Indian consumers.

Kohli also said Boba Bhai would prioritise formats that are not dependent on specialised chefs, allowing it to standardise food preparation and maintain consistency across a large store network.

“We don’t want to build a hotel or restaurant. We want to build a QSR where a 15-year-old can come in and still make the food taste the same,” he said.

Boba Bhai’s FY26 Snapshot

On the financial front, Boba Bhai reported a 145% jump in net revenue to around ₹70 Cr in FY26 from ₹28 Cr in the year-ago fiscal. Its net loss, however, widened 32% to ₹12.5 Cr in the fiscal under review from ₹9.5 Cr in FY25.

The startup’s growth was driven by an equal contribution from food and beverages, with both categories accounting for around 50% of revenue in FY26. It also recorded same-store sales growth of 30-40% during the fiscal.

Kohli said Boba Bhai has already crossed its entire FY26 revenue in the first half of FY27. The startup is currently clocking around ₹12.5 Cr in monthly revenue and has been growing 10-15% month-on-month, depending on seasonality.

In terms of channel mix, offline sales account for around 35% of revenue, while online channels contribute nearly 60%, according to the founder.

Kohli attributed the startup’s growth to execution, changing consumer eating-out habits and the timing of its entry into the market.

He believes the Korean food and bubble tea market in India remains largely fragmented, with no specialised player having scaled beyond 30-40 stores. While several restaurants offer bubble tea and Korean food as part of their wider menus, he believes there is room for organised, category-focused brands to build a larger presence.

Boba Bhai aims to eventually build a network of 1,000 stores in India. Our existing store network, supply-chain relationships and understanding of viable retail locations could help us expand faster, Kohli said.

Responding to a question about rising commodity prices, Kohli claimed that Boba Bhai remains largely self-sufficient in its domestic supply chain and does not expect geopolitical tensions to materially affect its operations.

item.title: Breach At External Vendor Exposes CoinDCX User Data
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: CoinDCX has informed its customers that unauthorised access at the crypto exchange’s messaging vendor Plotline exposed data of a “small…
item.content:encoded:
CoinDCX has informed its customers that unauthorised access at the crypto exchange’s messaging vendor Plotline exposed data of a “small number” of users last month.

For context, Plotline is a third-party vendor that CoinDCX uses to send in-app messages and notifications. 

In an email sent to the users, the platform said that breach occurred in two separate instances. The first incident occurred between October 24 and 26, and then again between October 30 and 31.

The crypto exchange, citing information available from Plotline, said that the data breach involved was limited to a “small number” of customers. As per the email, the unauthorised party accessed the names, email IDs and the names of banks added to users’ CoinDCX accounts. 

It did not disclose the number of affected users or specify whether any data was downloaded, copied or shared further. The exchange, however, informed the users that Plotline had no access to its internal databases, trade execution engines or user wallets. 

CoinDCX also reiterated that customer funds and wallets were “entirely secure and untouched”.

In a statement sent to Inc42, a CoinDCX spokesperson said, “Plotline, our third-party messaging vendor, experienced a security incident that exposed limited user contact details. CoinDCX’s systems and customer funds were not impacted at all. We have informed affected users and are strengthening our vendor risk controls”.

In its email to the users, CoinDCX also said it worked closely with Plotline to confirm that the incident had been fully contained. It has also initiated a review of Plotline’s security posture, data-minimisation practices and its internal vendor-risk processes.

The email did not identify the nature of the unauthorised access and the attacker. The incident comes as third-party service providers come under scrutiny amid a surge in AI-assisted cyberattacks. By writing exploit code on the fly and allowing threat actors to probe thousands of targets simultaneously, AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it.

This comes weeks after cryptocurrency exchange Binance also reported a major security breach, which impacted an estimated $6.3 Bn in assets. Earlier this month, researchers also flagged a malware at digital experience platform (DXP) Optimizely, which exposed visitors to potential theft of cryptocurrency, payment card details and browser data.

Earlier this month, India’s cybersecurity watchdog CERT-In also issued a critical warning to entities in the banking, financial services and insurance (BFSI) sector over an escalating campaign of AI-driven cyberattacks targeting payment and disbursement APIs.

item.content:encoded:
It has been a week of outages. From big tech giants like Microsoft and Apple to JPMorgan Chase and the US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), high-profile disruptions at key digital installations exposed how fragile the global digital infrastructure could be. 

While these incidents have not yet been established as AI-assisted cyberattacks, Nikesh Arora, CEO of Palo Alto Networks, one of the world’s largest cybersecurity companies, said that the events of week were far from a coincidence.

“So what the (cybersecurity) industry tried to warn enterprises about six months ago is here. The events of this week so far are not a coincidence. AI is making it easy for hackers to attack multiple customers,” said Arora in post on X.

Besides AI-assisted cyberattacks, he also blamed some of the outages on the a “deluge of patches” from vendors rushing to fix AI-discovered vulnerabilities. Noting that this “deluge” of patches was overwhelming IT teams, he urged the enterprises to test infrastructure across multiple AI models and revamp security operations centres.

His comments brought the spotlight back on the growing threat of AI-led cyberattacks. By automating reconnaissance, writing exploit code on the fly and allowing threat actors to probe thousands of targets simultaneously, AI is drastically compressing the time between discovering a flaw and weaponising it – leaving human defenders struggling to keep pace.

With new vulnerabilities surfacing every single day, how is AI making it harder for enterprises to keep pace with cyberattackers?

Cyberattacks In The AI Era

Cybersecurity expert Ritesh Bhatia, founder of cybersecurity platform V4WEB, believes that AI is not necessarily making cyberattacks more sophisticated. Instead, he says that the technology is accelerating techniques that attackers have been using for years.

According to him, the change is primarily visible in three areas: speed, scale and realism.

Tasks that earlier took days or months can now be completed in seconds, minutes or hours. Generative AI (GenAI) has also made phishing emails more convincing by eliminating grammatical errors that could previously alert recipients. Voice cloning and deepfakes further allow attackers to impersonate senior executives and issue fraudulent instructions.

Bhatia also flagged the problem of what he described as “shadow infrastructure” or “shadow assets” at large enterprises – systems that remain untracked, forgotten or outside regular IT monitoring. AI-assisted scanning can help attackers identify vulnerabilities in these overlooked systems, he adds.

Third-party vendors are another concern. Even large enterprises with strong cybersecurity teams often depend on smaller service providers that may not have comparable security capabilities. These vendors can become easier targets, particularly as AI lowers the barrier to learning hacking techniques.

“What previously required multiple individuals with specialised skills can now increasingly be handled by a single attacker. The bigger concern is the scale at which these operations can be replicated across organisations,” said Manohar Reddy Pagilla, threat researcher at CloudSEK.

He also added that the recent outages have highlighted the concentration risk across the global technology ecosystem. Pagilla further adds that from an attacker’s perspective, compromising a technology provider serving hundreds of organisations can be more rewarding than targeting each business individually.

Yet, the threat is no longer confined to external third-party vendors. As enterprises race to embed AI into their own workflows, they are inadvertently also expanding their exposure to cyberattacks from within.

The Widening Enterprise Attack Surface

Within enterprises, AI is opening up new fronts of vulnerability: accelerating how fast bug-laden software is shipped while simultaneously supercharging how quickly its code can be broken.

Developers can now generate and deploy vast volumes of code with minimal human scrutiny. This has increased the odds of critical flaws (in authentication, payment logic, and API integrations) slipping into production before being adequately reviewed.

Attackers, meanwhile, are using the same technology to probe multiple weaknesses at once, reverse-engineer applications, and map out attack paths in a fraction of the time it once took.

“The same capabilities that make our security testing faster can also make attackers substantially more effective,” said founder and CTO of Security Brigade Yash Kadakia.

Compounding the issue of unvetted code is the rapid spread of AI across day-to-day business operations, a trend Akshit Kaushik, cofounder and CBO of Mitigata, flags as a major new blind spot.

Enterprises are increasingly entrusting AI systems to handle customer queries, process refunds, generate code, and access internal databases. At the same time, employees are independently adopting unapproved “shadow AI” tools, often completely out of sight of security teams.

Every new integration creates a fresh entry point. Kaushik warns that attackers can hide malicious instructions inside seemingly routine emails and documents, manipulating enterprise AI assistants into leaking sensitive data or executing unauthorised actions.

To close these expanding gaps, he believes businesses must establish strict visibility and governance – tracking every AI tool deployed internally, auditing the data these systems can access, and ensuring their AI systems operate strictly within defined boundaries.

What Should Indian Enterprises Do?

For India, where banking, real-time payments, telecommunications, power, and public services are built on deeply interconnected digital infrastructure, the margin for error is shrinking fast. 

Security experts suggest that Indian enterprises must move beyond traditional perimeter defense and focus on three core pillars:

Sovereign Resilience and System Modernisation: Kaushal Bheda, director at Pelorus Technologies, warns that India’s reliance on foreign software and cloud platforms for critical infrastructure introduces a distinct layer of geopolitical and supply-chain risk. 

To insulate sensitive infrastructure, he believes that Indian enterprises should aggressively upgrade legacy systems, continuously monitor networks, and invest in indigenous security products designed and controlled within the country.

Proactive Cyber Hygiene and Threat Hunting: CloudSEK’s Pagilla advises organisations to immediately lock down their most common entry points: exposed credentials, unpatched internet-facing assets, excessive access permissions, and third-party vendor vulnerabilities. 

Rather than relying solely on internal alerts, he recommends augmenting existing security operations centres (SOCs) with external threat intelligence to detect and neutralise threats before they breach internal networks.

Board-Level Incident Readiness: V4WEB’s Bhatia argues that Indian companies must shift their mindset from pure prevention to inevitable recovery. “Death, taxes and cyberhacks are bound to happen,” he noted. 

According to Bhatia, Indian enterprises should regularly test data backups, rehearse restoration protocols and preparing clear crisis-communication playbooks for customers, partners, regulators and stock exchanges.

“Today, the most important thing that companies should prioritise is incident response. When an incident happens, don’t think that it won’t happen. Are you ready to respond to it? Are you resilient enough? Have you tested your backups? Are you able to restore them?” added Bhatia.

For Indian enterprises, therefore, the question is no longer simply whether AI can make cyberattacks more effective. It is whether their security teams, infrastructure, and leadership can respond at the exact same speed.

item.title: PB Fintech Cofounder Alok Bansal To Step Down From Executive Role
item.dc:creator: Team Inc42
item.description: Listed insurtech giant PB Fintech’s cofounder Alok Bansal is stepping down as the executive vice-chairman and whole-time director of the…
item.content:encoded:
Listed insurtech giant PB Fintech’s cofounder Alok Bansal is stepping down as the executive vice-chairman and whole-time director of the company. 

In a statement, the company said that Bansal’s tenure will expire on March 31, 2027. PB Fintech also said that he will be appointed as a non-executive director on the company’s board starting April 1, 2027, subject to shareholder approval.

In his resignation letter, Bansal cited his “personal desire” to step down from executive responsibilities as the reason for his departure. 

“PB Fintech and Policybazaar would not have been possible without Alok. He first shared his wish to step back five years ago, and I persuaded him to stay because I needed his support. I still do, and I am glad he will remain on our Board, while I understand his wish to step away from the day-to-day…,” said PB Fintech cofounder and CEO Yashish Dahiya.

Reminiscing on his 18 year-long tenure at the company, Bansal said, “… Founders are lucky to get most of the credit and sometimes, a few brickbats as well, but the reality is that it takes the collective energies of the team to build something meaningful. PB Fintech has achieved far greater scale than I ever imagined, thanks entirely to the dedication of our team, the trust of our customers, and the support of our investors and partners”.

An alumnus of IIM Calcutta, Bansal previously served at companies like Voltas, General Electric and Mahindra & Mahindra. He eventually cofounded Policybazaar (later PB Fintech) with Dahiya in 2008. 

Over his nearly two decades stint at the company, he oversaw the company’s rise into a multi-vertical insurtech company that closed Q2 FY27 with a net profit of ₹192.4 Cr and an operating revenue of ₹2,177.7 Cr. In a statement, the startup said that he was central to the company’s strategy, fundraising and investor relations, especially during its public listing in 2021.

The development comes amid a broader wave of cofounders quitting their startups and venture capital (VC) firms. Earlier this month, Unacademy Gaurav Munjal said that he was stepping down as the CEO of the edtech platform. Prior to this, Fireside Ventures’ cofounder and partner Vinay Singh also announced his departure from the investment firm after a nearly decade-long stint.

In June this year, cofounders Hari Menon and Vipul Parekh stepped down from their executive roles at the Tata Digital-owned BigBasket. In the same month, fintech platform Setu’s cofounder Nikhil Kumar resigned from the day-to-day operations of the Pine Labs-owned platform.

In April, used car marketplace Cars24’s cofounder and chief marketing officer (CMO) Gajendra Jangid also resigned from his executive role at the startup.
